p.title: Optimal Targeting in Fundraising: A Causal Machine-Learning Approach

ext.title: Optimal Targeting in Fundraising
ext.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.10251v3 [econ.EM], 29 Sep 2021 (dated September 30, 2021 on the title page). No journal appears in the text. AEA RCT Registry ID AEARCTR-0007581. The metadata hint matches the text.
ext.document_type: Working paper / arXiv preprint with online appendix (Appendices A-I)
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 4,079 lines of the file, including main text (pp. 1-34), references (pp. 34-39) and Online Appendix A-I (pp. 1-21). No Paul markup exists for this item (no markup files were supplied), so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: Can a charity raise more net donations (donations minus fundraising cost) by targeting an unconditional gift (small Dürer postcards mailed with a solicitation letter) to a subset of potential donors, using causal machine learning to learn an optimal targeting rule from a randomized field experiment, and does that rule generalize? Theory: charities face costly fundraising and donor overhead aversion (Rose-Ackerman 1982; Name-Correa and Yildirim 2013; Gneezy et al. 2014); the optimal rule targets "net donors" whose expected additional donation exceeds the marginal cost; heterogeneous motives (altruism, warm glow, reciprocity, sequential reciprocity) make gift effects heterogeneous across individuals.
ext.data: Natural field experiment in 2014 with a Catholic Church fundraiser in a German urban area (26% of residents are church members). Unit: individual church member (donor). Sample of 19,779 individuals: warm list (previous donors) N=2,354 (1,180 gift, 1,174 control); cold list (never donors) N=17,425 (2,283 gift, 15,142 control). Randomization stratified on list, gender, household type, quintiles of predicted baseline giving and age quintiles. Outcomes: donation amount in euro in the first year after the experiment (2015) and the first two years; donation dummy; net donation (donation minus gift variable cost, 1.16 euro). Covariates: (a) administrative records (gender, marital status, age, residency, donation history 2006-2015, per the text) and (b) Google Maps geospatial counts within 300 m (restaurants, supermarkets, medical, cultural facilities, churches) plus distances to station, city hall, main church and airport, travel time and elevation. External validity: 2015 follow-up experiment on a new warm-list sample (text says N=3,616; Table G.2 says 3,612), 50% gift probability; the 2015 sample is matched to 2014 by caliper propensity-score matching (radius 0.1). The text states donation records run 2006-2015 while also saying two post-experiment years were observed; the second year's dates are not reconciled in the text.
ext.method:
Potential-outcomes framework. CATE delta(x) and ATE identified under stratified randomization and SUTVA (Appendix B). Outcome-model/propensity nuisance estimation: logit for propensity, OLS for outcome regressions (Table D.1), combined into an augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) score (Eq. 3-4). Optimal targeting rule estimated directly via Athey and Wager (2021) empirical welfare maximization, using exact policy-learning trees of Zhou, Athey and Wager (2018) with search depth two (policytree R package). Gains evaluated by 20-fold cross-validation of out-of-sample net donations versus all-gift, no-gift and random-gift benchmarks. Descriptive heterogeneity: sorted-effects approach (Chernozhukov, Fernandez-Val and Luo 2018) with multiplier-bootstrap bands, plus best linear predictor test with causal forest (Chernozhukov et al. 2020). Data-type ablations (socioeconomic, donation history, geospatial, combinations). Sensitivity to depth one and three exact trees, CART (fixed and cross-validated depth), weighted logit (baseline and flexible), logit lasso, classification forest; nuisance robustness via population propensity and cross-fitted lasso (Tables I.1-I.4). Identification of the targeting gain does not require identifying the causal effect of each characteristic; trees indicate correlations only.
Identification strategy: random assignment of the gift within strata (Zi), exogenous of potential outcomes conditional on Zi, 0 < p(z) < 1; heterogeneity variables Xi are not needed for identification.
ext.scope: Population: church members in one German urban area, targeted by one Catholic Church fundraiser with an annual solicitation mailing, split into warm (past donors) and cold (never donors) lists. Institution: a single religious charity; religious giving is the largest private giving category in Germany (about 35% of private giving per the text, citing Deutscher Spendenrat 2016). Era: 2014 treatment with 2015 (and second-year) outcomes; 2015 follow-up experiment on warm list. The paper states the findings may be specific to the setting.

key_findings.finding: Gift ATE on donations (first year): warm list +1.21 to +1.24 euro, not significant. Net of the 1.16 euro gift cost: +0.05 to +0.08 euro, not significant. Cold list ATE +0.19 euro (significant); net of cost -0.97 euro per donor, so the all-gift rule loses money in the cold list.
key_findings.numbers: warm ATE 1.21-1.24 (SE 1.15-1.25); warm net 0.05-0.08; cold ATE 0.19 (SE 0.07-0.10); cold net -0.97 (SE 0.07-0.10); preferred AIPW warm ATE 1.22, net 0.06

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity: sorted effects show substantial individual variation in warm-list gift effects; 45% of warm-list individuals have estimated effects above the 1.16 euro cost. Effects range from +17.99 euro (95th percentile responders) to -11.59 euro (5th percentile). In the cold list, effects exceed cost only above the 92nd percentile and are small.
key_findings.numbers: warm: 45% above cost; 5th pct -11.59 euro; responsive individuals +17.99 euro; cold: 5th pct -0.73, 95th pct +1.38 euro

key_findings.finding: Best linear predictor test with causal forest detects significant effect heterogeneity in the warm list and none in the cold list.
key_findings.location: Section 5.2 and Table E.3 (p.21; Appendix p.12)

key_findings.finding: Warm list optimal rule (cross-validated out-of-sample): gift is assigned to 33% of warm-list individuals; expected net donations 17.61 euro, which is 2.14 euro (13.8%) above all-gift, 2.20 euro (14.3%) above no-gift, and 2.17 euro (14.1%) above random-gift, all significant.
key_findings.numbers: share treated 0.33; net donation 17.61 euro (SE 0.97); vs all-gift 2.14*** (0.82); vs no-gift 2.20*** (0.81); vs random 2.17*** (0.58)

key_findings.finding: Secondary outcomes (warm list): donation probability in first year is +0.025 (significant at 5%) vs no-gift, with no significant difference from the all-gift rule; net donations over two years are 32.94 euro, +2.33 vs all-gift and +3.75 vs no-gift, so the gains persist and there is no evidence of pull-forward.
key_findings.numbers: donation probability 1st year 0.503; vs no-gift 0.025**; two-year net donations 32.94 euro; +2.33* vs all-gift; +3.75*** vs no-gift; two-year probability 0.582

key_findings.finding: Cold list optimal rule assigns the gift to only 1.4% of cold-list individuals. Expected net donation 0.15 euro, essentially equal to no-gift (-0.005, not significant), and significantly above all-gift (0.97 euro) and random-gift (0.48 euro). The paper concludes the gift should not be sent to cold-list individuals at all.
key_findings.numbers: share treated 0.014; net donation 0.15***; vs all-gift 0.97*** (0.10); vs no-gift -0.005 (0.012); vs random 0.48*** (0.05)

key_findings.finding: Warm-list targeted (net donor) vs non-targeted (net receiver) characteristics: targeted donors gave more before the experiment (average 4.10 vs 3.90 prior donations; 130.98 vs 123.39 euro total prior donations), live at lower elevation (308.66 vs 321.38 m), and have more restaurants, churches and cultural facilities nearby. Socioeconomic differences are small. Sample: 787 targeted vs 1,567 non-targeted.
key_findings.numbers: elevation std diff 157.80; cultural facilities 0.240 vs 0.050 (std diff 32.27); female share 0.507 vs 0.539 (std diff 6.46)

key_findings.finding: Cold-list targeted vs non-targeted: targeted individuals live closer to city hall, main station and airport, have fewer restaurants nearby (5.48 vs 10.40), and are more often female (0.558 vs 0.503) and single (0.713 vs 0.642). Sample: 251 targeted vs 17,174 non-targeted.
key_findings.numbers: distance to city hall 1.364 vs 2.816 km (std diff 103.02); restaurants 5.482 vs 10.40 (std diff 57.08)

key_findings.finding: Data needed: the warm-list rule using only geospatial data (17.40 euro expected net donation, +1.92** vs all-gift, +1.98** vs no-gift) or only donation history (17.20 euro, +1.73** and +1.79**) performs about as well as the baseline (17.61 euro). Socioeconomic data alone do not beat the three benchmarks (15.71 euro; differences insignificant). Adding socioeconomic data does not improve the rules. Cold list: geospatial-only rule gives 0.15 euro, the same as the baseline.
key_findings.numbers: warm geospatial-only 17.40; donation-history-only 17.20; socioeconomic-only 15.71 with vs no-gift 0.27 (insignificant); cold geospatial-only 0.15 with vs no-gift -0.005

key_findings.finding: External validity over time: the 2014 rule applied to a caliper-matched 2015 warm-list sample (radius 0.1) yields 19.85 euro expected net donation, +2.64* vs all-gift and +2.30** vs no-gift, and 35.6% treated. Applied to the full 2015 sample it yields 17.16 euro with no significant gain over all-gift (-0.88) or no-gift (+0.45). The text says the 2015 average gift effect is 1.33 euro vs 0.08 in 2014.

Caliper sensitivity: the 2014 rule significantly beats no-gift up to a caliper radius of 0.25; beating all-gift is harder because the gift raises average net donations in the full 2015 sample. Above 0.1 the effects are no longer statistically significant but remain positive in expectation.
key_findings.location: Section 5.6 and Appendix H, Figure H.1 (p.31-32)
key_findings.numbers: significance against no-gift holds to caliper 0.25; radius 0.1 is the standard

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity: in the warm list, the baseline exact policy tree (depth 2) dominates the alternative estimators, which yield lower net donations. Depth-1 trees and flexible logit have the lowest performance. The cross-validated-depth CART is the only alternative that significantly beats both all-gift and no-gift (17.40 euro, +1.93** and +1.98**). In the cold list, logit lasso and cross-validated CART are 0.01 euro higher, but the no-gift conclusion holds.
key_findings.numbers: CV-CART warm 17.40 (+1.93 vs all-gift); flexible logit 16.28; depth-1 tree 15.05; cold logit lasso/CV-CART +0.01 euro

key_findings.finding: Nuisance-parameter robustness: using the population propensity score or cross-fitted logit-lasso nuisances gives essentially identical results (warm 17.63 and 17.35 euro expected net donation; cold 0.15 euro).
key_findings.numbers: population propensity: warm 17.63, +2.15***, +2.21***; cross-fitted lasso: warm 17.35, +1.85***, +1.79**

key_findings.finding: Example decision trees: the warm-list tree splits first on maximum prior donation (101.76 euro) and home elevation (313.55 m). The cold-list tree splits on number of restaurants within 300 m (5), distance to city hall (1.28 km) and distance to airport (3.06 km). The text warns that trees show correlations, not causal effects.
key_findings.location: Section 5.4 and Figure F.1 (p.26-27; Appendix p.13)
key_findings.numbers: warm leaves: gift 4.94 euro (N=758), 81.13 euro (N=48); cold leaf 21.44 euro (N=58)

measures: Donation amount in euro, first year after the experiment (2015), and cumulative first two years
Donation dummy (any donation), first year and first two years
Net donation = donation minus gift variable cost (1.16 euro for the gift treatment; letter costs 0.43 euro)
Expected net donation under a targeting rule P(pi), and excess net donation versus all-gift (Q1), no-gift (Q-1) and random-gift (QR) benchmarks
Share of individuals assigned the gift by the rule
CATE / sorted effects (euro); best linear predictor heterogeneity loadings
Standardized differences (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983 threshold 20) for balance and targeted-vs-non-targeted comparisons

Geospatial counts within 300 m (restaurants, supermarkets, medical, cultural facilities, churches) and distances (km) and travel time (minutes) to station, city hall, main church and airport; elevation (m)
limitations: Authors state that findings 'may well be specific to the setting' (one Catholic Church fundraiser, one German urban area, one annual letter with a folded-card gift).

The optimal targeting rule identifies the policy gain, not the causal effect of each characteristic; trees show correlations, and unobserved variables (e.g., income, willingness to give) may drive the heterogeneity (Section 5.4).
The gain estimates are cross-validated (K=20) rather than from a fresh holdout sample; external validity is tested only on one 2015 follow-up with warm-list individuals.

External validity holds only when the new sample is similar to the training sample: the 2014 rule works against no-gift up to caliper 0.25, but against all-gift only for similar samples; the full 2015 sample shows no significant gains (Table 8).

Cold-list results have far fewer treated individuals in the rule (1.4%, 251 individuals), and depth-three exact trees are infeasible in the cold list (Table I.2 note), so the cold-list tree comparison is limited.
Data scope: the authors use only covariates the charity can collect (administrative records and Google Maps data); richer data could change results (Section 5.5 and Conclusion).
Robustness checks use parametric nuisance estimators (logit and OLS); the authors note the AIPW estimator requires consistent and fast-converging nuisance estimators (Section 4.3).

Internal inconsistencies in the text: the 2015 follow-up sample is 3,616 in the text but 3,612 in Table G.2 and 1,806+1,806 in Table G.1; the Table 8 note cites an expected 17.01 euro while the table shows 19.85; the text says donation records cover 2006-2015 but also refers to two post-experiment years.

short_quotes.quote: machine-learning-based optimal targeting allows the charity to substantially increase donations net of fundraising costs relative to uniform benchmarks
We conclude that charities not engaging in optimal targeting waste significant resources.
We conclude that the fundraiser should not target cold-list individuals at all.

ext.identification: Random assignment of the gift stratified on list, gender, household type, quintiles of predicted baseline willingness to give and age quintiles; SUTVA; overlap 0 < p(z) < 1 (Appendix B). Targeting gains are identified from the AIPW score; no need to observe heterogeneity variables for identification.
ext.theory: Charities are public-goods providers facing costly fundraising and donor overhead aversion. Targeting a costly instrument at net donors (expected gain above marginal cost) maximizes net donations (Name-Correa and Yildirim 2013). Donor heterogeneity from altruism, warm glow and reciprocity (Falk 2007; Falk et al. 2018) makes gift effects heterogeneous.

rel.summary_md:
Cagala, Glogowsky, Rincke and Strittmatter ran a natural field experiment in 2014 with a Catholic Church fundraiser in one German city (N=19,779 church members). A small gift (postcards, cost 1.16 euro) was randomly assigned with the solicitation letter, stratified by warm list (past donors, N=2,354) and cold list (never donors, N=17,425). Sending the gift to everyone barely paid for itself on the warm list (net +0.06 euro, not significant) and lost money on the cold list (-0.97 euro per person). Gift effects varied widely across warm-list donors, from -11.59 to +17.99 euro between the 5th and 95th percentiles. The authors used AIPW scores and a depth-2 exact policy tree (Athey-Wager policy learning) to learn who should get the gift. Under 20-fold cross-validation, the rule sent the gift to 33% of the warm list and raised expected net donations by about 2.1-2.2 euro (about 14%) over all-gift, no-gift and random assignment. On the cold list the rule chose almost nobody (1.4%). Geospatial covariates alone did about as well as the full set of covariates. Applied to a new 2015 sample, the rule only helped where the 2015 donors closely resembled the 2014 donors (caliper match 0.1). On the full 2015 sample it showed no significant gain.

What this means for Paul's systems: a targeting rule for a costly treatment is only justified when it beats uniform and random benchmarks out of sample, and that requires randomized variation in the treatment. Melange's money allocators and Terrier's canvass potential score both target on heterogeneity that is assumed, through hand-set response curves, multipliers and weights. Neither is learned from a randomized assignment. The paper describes the experiment and benchmark test the system lacks. It does not validate any of the system's constants. Its setting (individual charitable donors) also differs from the system's targets: legislators for Melange, and voters for Terrier.

bearings.paper_claim: A targeting rule for a costly instrument earns its keep only when its out-of-sample net gain beats all-treat, no-treat and random benchmarks. The warm-list rule gained +2.14, +2.20 and +2.17 euro (about 14%, cross-validated). In the full 2015 sample the gain over all-gift and no-gift vanished (-0.88 and +0.45, not significant). Heterogeneity was identified only from randomized gift assignment (AIPW plus policy tree).
bearings.system_side: CELF greedy allocates a $2.5M pot in $500 chunks to maximize modeled winnability. Per-member returns come from the design-set saturating pflip money term, scaled by pressure_mult and the competitiveness multiplier. Greedy is certified optimal only within the model (fixed-state certificate). No realized-outcome comparison is made against uniform, random or no-spend allocation.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transferable part is the evaluation design: benchmark-relative, net-of-cost gains measured on held-out units under randomized treatment. The effect sizes do not transfer, because the paper studies a 1.16-euro gift to German church donors in 2014-15, not PAC dollars to Members of Congress. FEC limits and the absence of randomization mean the system cannot directly replicate the paper's identification. Any optimizer gain stays model-internal (UNVERIFIED per DE-062) until outcomes are scored against a benchmark allocation.

bearings.paper_claim: Where a treatment works better is an empirical CATE question. Even after detection with a causal forest (BLP loading 0.959 on the warm list, none on the cold list), the learned rule failed to carry over to a population that differed: no significant gain on the full 2015 sample, and significance only up to caliper 0.1 against all-gift. Trees show correlates, not the causal role of a covariate.
bearings.paper_location: Section 5.2, Table E.3; Section 5.4; Section 5.6 and Figure H.1
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0*exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0) scales effective dollars, assuming dollars buy more in competitive seats. Brain records it as owner judgment, uncalibrated (D-104..D-108), default ON.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is about method, not legislators or PVI. It shows how heterogeneous dollar effectiveness would have to be established (randomized variation plus a heterogeneity test plus checks of transfer to a new population). It gives no evidence for or against the PVI shape. Do not cite it as support for c.

bearings.paper_claim: Responsiveness to a costly contact is heterogeneous and is not the same as baseline propensity. Warm-list gift effects ranged from -11.59 to +17.99 euro, and only 45% of warm-list donors exceeded cost. Cheap geospatial covariates (300 m counts, distances, elevation) learned a rule as good as the full set (17.40 vs 17.61 euro). Socioeconomic data alone did not beat the benchmarks (15.71 euro).
bearings.system_side: potential = (wp*(1-|2s-1|)*t + (1-wp)*s*(1-t))*(1+wi*i), with hand-set wp=wi=0.5. Persuasion and mobilization value are assumed from the support level and turnout propensity, not estimated contact effects. Knocked doors with saved results exist but are not used to learn response.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies to individual-level targeting of a costly contact, which is structurally closest to Terrier. It does not transfer the paper's numbers, because those come from charitable gifts rather than canvass persuasion or GOTV. A learned rule would need randomized contact assignment (for example a held-out control list per turf), not the saved walk results, which are selected on who was knocked. The paper also warns that a rule fit in one year or district may not carry over to the next.

bearings.paper_claim: Policy gains are identified from randomized assignment through the AIPW score, without needing to identify each covariate's causal effect. The paper's cross-validated gains were then checked against a new-year sample, where they held only for similar units.
bearings.system_side: The H1 and H2 contracts are explicitly limited to forecasting (claim_scope 'receptivity_forecast_only_not_spending_effects'). The system has no design that identifies the effect of spending or contact.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper shows the missing design: randomized treatment within strata. That is the precondition for upgrading the contract from forecasting to spending-effect evidence. This is feasible for Terrier contacts or CU outreach logs. It is not feasible for statutory PAC contributions to legislators. The paper used 20-fold CV rather than a single-look holdout, which is weaker than the system's discipline.

bearings.paper_claim: Treating everyone above a ranking (all-gift) can be net-negative or near zero (cold list -0.97 euro, warm list +0.06 euro). Ranking by baseline giving is not the same as ranking by response: targeted warm donors differed only modestly in prior giving (130.98 vs 123.39 euro).
bearings.system_side: Funds the top 133 of 533 members from a flat $2.0M pot in proportion to the blended influence score. The score ordering is assumed to equal funding priority, with no response or cost term.
bearings.code_ref: Moneyball Main Version - Blended.xlsx Blended Model col U (no Python producer; fec/apply_alloc_cap.py not applied)
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is conceptual. The paper's warning is that a level ranking (influence, past giving) is not an effect ranking. The magnitudes come from donors, not legislators. It supports asking that the proportional allocator be compared against a uniform or random benchmark. It does not show that the allocator is wrong.

gaps_exposed: No randomized or held-out variation in any costly treatment (PAC dollars, outreach, canvass contact). Every response heterogeneity in the allocators and in Terrier is an owner-set prior, not an estimated CATE.
No benchmark-relative evaluation: neither the optimizer nor the workbook allocator reports realized, net-of-cost gain against all-fund, no-fund or random-fund allocations.

Terrier's untapped-potential score targets on support level and turnout propensity. It has no estimate of who responds to a knock, and saved walk results are selected (non-random), so they cannot identify response.

There is no check that a targeting rule carries over to a changed population (new Congress, new district, new cycle), which is the paper's 2015 caliper test. The paper's rule lost significance on the full new sample.
There is no test of which covariate families (cheap geospatial vs administrative vs socioeconomic) are sufficient for targeting, which matters for Terrier's vendor-field costs.
flags: Do not cite this paper as evidence that dollars buy more in competitive seats or that reciprocity holds. It studies charitable donors, not legislators, and reciprocity is NOT validated (D-104..D-108).

Any figure quoted from it must name its window and denominator. Examples: 2014 treatment with 2015 first-year outcomes; warm list N=2,354, of whom 787 were targeted; cold list N=17,425; the 2015 follow-up sample is 3,616 in the text and 3,612 in Table G.2 (an internal inconsistency).
The headline +14% gain is cross-validated in-sample (K=20). On the full 2015 sample, the gain over all-gift was not significant (-0.88 euro). Quote both, never the 14% alone.
Any agent-built Terrier or allocator benchmark inspired by this paper stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
The paper makes no SNA, LDA-edge or per-edge normalization argument, so the rejected-proposal flags do not apply.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, so no note is stale. It partly cuts against his ROI framing of money (flip-model and break-even positions): uniformly applied, the costly instrument barely covered its cost, and it paid only when targeted on response that had been learned from randomized data. It partly supports his joint-optimizer position that a learned policy should eventually replace hand-built greedy targeting. The paper's sense of 'learned', though, is causal policy learning from an RCT, not GCOMB-style learning over graphs. On Terrier, Paul highlighted the Kalla & Broockman canvass protocol. This paper adds the complementary point: who to contact should be estimated from randomized contact, not assumed from support level and turnout propensity.

related.why: Also estimates returns to targeting a persuasion treatment on heterogeneous effects versus a uniform message, which is the same benchmark-relative question in political persuasion.
Microtargeting persuasion experiment: tests whether tailoring a treatment to individual traits beats a uniform treatment, which parallels the paper's policy-tree versus all-gift comparison.

Randomized field experiment on a costly political instrument (contributions to obtain access). This is the kind of identification the paper says a targeting rule needs, and it concerns the system's actual target.
Shows that treatment effects (returns to moderation) depend on where voters are, the same heterogeneity-depends-on-population lesson as the paper's failure to carry over to the 2015 sample.
Agent-based proof of principle that micro-targeting beats broadcast; this paper supplies the field-experimental counterpart with real net-of-cost numbers.
